title: Memory & I/O Optimization
blurb: Tests why read chunk size dominates I/O cost, why OS buffering is a weaker and sometimes negative lever, when mmap helps and when it doesn't, what __slots__ saves, and why preallocating a Python list is a myth while preallocating a NumPy array is not.

refLinks.label: §54.2.1 Read Chunk Size: The Dominant, First-Order Effect
§54.2.2 OS-Level Buffering: A Real, Much Smaller, Sometimes Negative Effect
§54.2.3 Memory-Mapped Files: A Genuine Win, With an Honest Asterisk

questions.prompt: Why is reading a file one byte at a time so slow?
options: Small reads always bypass the OS page cache and go straight to disk.
Disks can only deliver data in single bytes when asked to.
Each read() call has a fixed cost, paid here once per byte read.
Python decodes each byte as Unicode before returning it to the caller.
questions.explanation: A Python call, a system call and buffer bookkeeping happen on every read, whatever its size. At 1 byte per call, that overhead is paid 210 million times for a 210 MB file.

refLinks.label: §54.2.1 Read Chunk Size: The Dominant, First-Order Effect

questions.prompt: Chunk size 1 took 8,322.8 ms and chunk size 1 MB took 13.7 ms for the same file. About how many times faster is 1 MB? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 8,322.8 / 13.7 = 607.5, over 600x, for moving the exact same bytes.

questions.prompt: Memory is tight. What chunk size does Procedure 54.1 suggest instead of reading line by line or byte by byte?
options: A moderate size, 64 KB to 1 MB
Exactly the size of one disk sector, 512 bytes
The whole file in a single read call
The smallest size possible, one byte
questions.explanation: Going smaller saves little memory but multiplies call overhead. A moderate chunk keeps memory bounded without paying per-byte costs.

questions.prompt: With the read chunk fixed at 1 MB, what did raising buffering= to 16 MB do?
options: It caused the read loop to fail partway.
It made no measurable difference at all.
It made reads about 5x slower.
It made reads about 5x faster than the other settings.
questions.explanation: 0, 4 KB and 1 MB buffering all measured about 13 ms, while 16 MB took 66.4 ms. Buffering is a weaker, second-order lever, and over-tuning it can hurt.

refLinks.label: §54.2.2 OS-Level Buffering: A Real, Much Smaller, Sometimes Negative Effect

questions.prompt: What order of effort does the chapter recommend for file reads?
options: Switch every read to mmap first, then tune the chunk size.
Tune OS buffering first, since it applies to every read in the program.
Fix application chunk size first, then consider OS buffering, and measure it.
Increase both chunk size and buffering together, as far as memory allows.
questions.explanation: Chunk size is the first-order effect. Once reads are large, OS read-ahead has little left to amortise, and bigger isn't always better.

refLinks.label: §54.2.2 OS-Level Buffering: A Real, Much Smaller, Sometimes Negative Effect

questions.prompt: Where does mmap's advantage come from?
options: It reads the whole file into RAM when it is opened.
No system call per access, once the pages are already cached.
It skips page faults on the very first access to each page.
It compresses the file's pages in memory to save bandwidth.
questions.explanation: seek() plus read() makes a system call every time, even for cached data. With mmap, a cached page is an ordinary memory access. The first touch still faults either way.

refLinks.label: §54.2.3 Memory-Mapped Files: A Genuine Win, With an Honest Asterisk

questions.prompt: On a single cold pass of 50,000 random reads, mmap ran at 0.82x of seek() plus read(). Why wasn't it faster?
options: The file was too small for mmap to be used at all.
First accesses still page-fault, and slicing costs extra.
The test was wrong, since mmap is always faster than read().
mmap disables the OS page cache for the mapped file.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this an honest negative result. mmap's win only appears once pages are resident.

refLinks.label: §54.2.3 Memory-Mapped Files: A Genuine Win, With an Honest Asterisk

questions.prompt: After warming the cache, seek() plus read() took 90.3 ms and mmap 7.2 ms. What is mmap's speedup? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 90.3 / 7.2 = 12.5, entirely from avoiding a system call per access on cached data.

questions.prompt: Which access pattern does Procedure 54.2 say mmap suits?
options: Writing a log file one line at a time, as events arrive
Reading a file that is much larger than available RAM, once
A single sequential pass over a large file, read once
Repeated or random access to a file whose pages stay cached
questions.explanation: For a single sequential pass, a plain chunked read is simpler and just as fast. mmap pays off when the same pages are hit repeatedly.

questions.prompt: What does __slots__ remove from each instance?
options: The per-instance __dict__ for attributes
The object's reference count and type pointer
The class's methods, which are copied into each object
The garbage collector's tracking of the object
questions.explanation: __slots__ gives fixed storage for the declared attributes instead of a dict. Methods live on the class, and every object keeps its header.

questions.prompt: Objects took 120 bytes each without __slots__ and 88 bytes with it. What percentage of memory did __slots__ save? Give one decimal place.

options: When the class has a fixed, known set of attributes
When the class needs attributes added at runtime
When you hold millions of instances of a simple record
When memory use decides whether the data fits in RAM
questions.explanation: __slots__ trades flexibility for memory. It can also clash with non-slots base classes in multiple inheritance. The other three are where it fits best.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't preallocating a Python list with [None] * n beat append()?
options: Preallocated lists are stored on disk instead of in memory.
CPython already over-allocates, amortising append's resizes.
append() is compiled to C, but indexing is interpreted.
[None] * n creates n separate None objects, which is slow.
questions.explanation: The list grows in chunks larger than needed, so append is amortised O(1). The manual trick hand-rolls what the interpreter already does. None is a single shared object.

questions.prompt: Where is preallocation a real, large win?
options: NumPy arrays, where np.append in a loop copies every time
Python sets, when they are used for membership tests
Python dicts, when the keys are known ahead of time
Python lists, when they hold more than a million items
questions.explanation: np.append makes a new array each call, so filling a preallocated np.empty(n) is much faster. CPython's list growth makes the trick pointless for lists.

questions.prompt: Why was the list comprehension fastest of the three ways to build a list?
options: It runs in parallel on several CPU cores at once.
It preallocates the list behind the scenes, unlike append().
It skips building a list and returns a lazy generator.
It skips the .append lookup, using dedicated bytecode.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses the reason is unrelated to allocation. 135.9 ms against 149.1 and 142.4 ms came from cheaper bytecode, not memory strategy.

questions.prompt: A service reads 2 GB log files line by line with readline(), then looks up random offsets in a separate index file many times per request. What does the chapter suggest?
options: mmap both files, since mmap is always faster for large files.
Raise buffering= to 64 MB for both and keep the reads as they are.
Read both files one byte at a time, to keep memory as low as possible.
Chunked reads for logs, mmap for the index.
questions.explanation: Sequential log reading wants a moderate chunk size. Repeated random index lookups on cached pages are mmap's best case. Big buffers were a negative result, and byte reads were the slowest of all.

bookExercises.prompt: State, in one sentence each, why chunk size 1 and chunk size 1MB differ by more than 600x when reading the identical file, and why the `buffering=` parameter's effect is so much smaller than chunk size's.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Chunk size 1 forces one Python-level `read()` system call per single byte (~210 million calls for a 210MB file), each carrying fixed system-call overhead, while 1MB chunks need only ~200 calls total. The overhead is paid per-call, so shrinking the number of calls by six orders of magnitude removes almost all of it. The `buffering=` parameter only adjusts an additional internal buffering layer on top of already-large `read()` calls, so its effect is marginal once the dominant per-call overhead is already eliminated by chunk size.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain why `mmap` measured *slower* than `seek()`+`read()` on a single cold pass in this chapter's Worked Example, even though `mmap` is described as a performance optimization.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `mmap` measured slower on a cold pass because the file's pages aren't yet resident in memory. The very first access to each page still triggers a page fault, forcing the OS to load it from disk, which is at least as expensive as a direct `read()` call plus adds `mmap`'s own setup overhead. `mmap`'s advantage only appears on repeated/warm access, where already-resident pages are reached with an ordinary memory access instead of a fresh system call.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 54.1 as a base, write a version that also reports the number of `read()` calls made, and predict (before running it) roughly how many calls a 50MB file would need at a 256KB chunk size.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: At 256KB chunks, a 50MB file needs approximately $50 \times 1024 \times 1024 / (256 \times 1024) = 200$ `read()` calls (50MB / 256KB ≈ 200).

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague's class holds 2,000,000 instances of a `Point3D` class with three float attributes and no need for dynamic attributes. Using this chapter's 26.7% reduction figure as a guide, estimate the memory saved by adding `__slots__`, given that the regular-class measurement in this chapter used 120 bytes/object for a two-attribute class.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The chapter's own class used 120 bytes/object regular vs. 88 bytes/object with `__slots__` for a two-attribute class (26.7% reduction). A three-float-attribute `Point3D` would have a somewhat different absolute byte count, but applying the same proportional reduction to 2,000,000 instances at roughly 120 bytes/object regular gives ~240MB regular vs. ~176MB with `__slots__`, a savings on the order of 60-65MB, scaling with the actual per-object byte counts for a three-attribute class.

bookExercises.prompt: Modify Listing 54.4 to measure `np.append`-in-a-loop versus a preallocated `np.empty(n)` array filled by index, for 100,000 elements, and report which pattern this chapter's Trade-offs section predicts should win.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: This chapter's Trade-offs section predicts negligible difference between preallocation and append-growth for a plain Python `list` (149.1ms vs. 142.4ms measured). CPython's amortised growth strategy already avoids the repeated-reallocation cost preallocation is meant to prevent. `np.append`-in-a-loop is a different case: unlike Python lists, `np.append` creates an entirely new array on every call (no amortised growth), so it should lose badly to a preallocated `np.empty(n)` filled by index. The "preallocation doesn't matter" finding is specific to Python lists, not NumPy arrays.

bookExercises.prompt: A teammate proposes converting every small class in a data-loading pipeline to use `__slots__` "for consistency," including a `Config` class that user code sometimes monkey-patches with extra attributes at runtime. Using this chapter's Procedure 54.3, write the two-sentence case against doing this uniformly.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `__slots__` prevents adding arbitrary attributes at runtime. A `Config` class that user code monkey-patches with extra attributes would break immediately once `__slots__` is added, since assigning an attribute not declared in `__slots__` raises an `AttributeError`. Applying `__slots__` "for consistency" without checking each class's actual usage pattern risks breaking legitimate dynamic-attribute use cases for a memory saving that only matters at genuinely large object counts.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's list-preallocation result is described as "genuinely false for CPython specifically... does not generalize to every container or every language." Propose one other container (Python or otherwise) where you'd expect preallocation to matter, and justify why its growth strategy differs from CPython `list`'s.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Fixed-size arrays in lower-level languages like C++ (`std::vector`) or Java (`ArrayList`) still benefit from preallocation (`reserve()`), because unlike CPython's list (whose growth is already amortised at the interpreter level), these containers' default growth strategies can involve real reallocation-and-copy costs that `reserve()` explicitly avoids by allocating the final capacity upfront. The difference is which layer already amortises growth by default.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the `mmap` module documentation's section on `ACCESS_READ` versus `ACCESS_WRITE` versus `ACCESS_COPY`. Explain in a sentence or two how a write-heavy access pattern would change this chapter's cold-versus-warm analysis, which was measured read-only.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. A write-heavy access pattern (`ACCESS_WRITE`) would change the cold-pass comparison because `mmap` writes are typically deferred/lazily flushed by the OS's page cache, potentially making `mmap` writes appear faster than they truly are until an explicit flush/sync, while `seek()`+`write()` calls involve explicit, more predictable write-through semantics. A fair write-heavy comparison would need to account for when data is actually guaranteed durable on disk, not just when the Python call returns.
